transcript.content: Hi, welcome in, and thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been going on that brought you in to see me?

Yeah, thanks. I guess... well, the main thing is I just get pulled off track by literally every little sound or thought. Like, I’ll be trying to work on a job application, right? Because I've been trying to find something since this warehouse gig my buddy told me about fell through. Which is honestly probably for the best anyway, since it was way out by the highway and my car—well, it's my mom's old Honda, I just borrow it sometimes—has this really weird rattling noise in the dashboard. I keep meaning to look up a YouTube video to figure out what's rattling in there, maybe a loose clip or something. 

Actually, wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the applications. Yeah, so I'll sit down to fill one out, and then a car drives by outside, or my phone lights up, or I just get some random idea—like fixing the Honda—and suddenly I'm doing something completely different before I even notice I stopped working. It's just happening all the time.
Can you tell me how far back you can remember having this kind of distractibility—did it start in childhood, or is this something that's more new for you, say in the last few months?

Oh, man, no, it's definitely not new. It goes way, way back. Like, even in elementary school, my teachers were always moving my seat around the room because I'd be talking out of turn constantly. And I was always forgetting my homework, or if we had to do worksheets in class, I'd just rush right through them and make all these dumb careless mistakes just to be done with it. 

I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Davis, she actually moved my desk right up against hers so she could watch me. She had this giant glass jar of jelly beans on her desk, like the kind you're supposed to guess the number of to win a prize at a fair? But she just ate them all day while we worked. Mostly the black licorice ones. Which is crazy because those are literally the worst ones. My grandpa used to eat those, actually. He’d keep a bag of them in the glovebox of his truck. We used to go fishing in that truck all the time down by the creek, and it always smelled like peppermint and old motor oil... 

Wait, sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, when it started. Yeah, so it’s been happening pretty much my whole life, definitely not just the last few months.
Aside from the distractibility, do you often feel physically restless—like needing to get up, fidget, or move around—or find yourself acting or speaking impulsively before thinking things through?

Yeah, totally. It's like... especially since I can't really play soccer like I used to, sitting around the house just makes me feel like I’m literally crawling out of my skin. 

I miss playing, honestly. We used to have this Sunday pickup game over at the park on 4th street. The grass there was always super patchy, though. Like, you'd go to kick the ball and just take out a huge chunk of dry dirt. I actually ruined a brand new pair of cleats there once. They were these bright neon green ones I got on clearance at that sporting goods store over by the mall. I don't even usually wear neon, but they were like sixty percent off. Have you been to that mall lately, by the way? Half the stores are boarded up now, it's pretty depressing. The pretzel stand in the food court is still open, thank god. I could eat those cinnamon sugar pretzels every single day. My buddy works there and sometimes he gives me the leftover ones at closing... 

Wait, sorry. Restless. Right. Yeah, so since I'm not playing soccer to burn that off, I just end up pacing from room to room all day. Just walking back and forth through the house because I can't stand just sitting there.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports lifelong (since elementary school) pervasive inattentive symptoms (distractibility by minor external/internal stimuli, careless mistakes, forgetfulness, difficulty sustaining task completion) combined with hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (subjective restlessness, inability to remain seated, pacing, talking out of turn in childhood). Symptoms are present across multiple settings (school, home, work/job applications) and have caused functional impairment (school discipline, occupational difficulty completing applications). Both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptom clusters are simultaneously present and clinically significant, supporting the Combined Presentation (F90.2) rather than a single-domain presentation.
